hero.heading: How OpenWOP compares on workflow orchestration

intro.heading: Capabilities, not scores
intro.body: This page maps concrete orchestration capabilities against representative products in each category. We mark competitors by whether a capability **ships today** — not by a quality rating or ranking. Where we lead, it is usually on the axes the whole field is still weak on: replay and fork-from-any-step, running without a determinism tax, evaluation-gated publishing, per-run cost attribution, and a real human-in-the-loop ladder.

matrix.heading: Orchestration capabilities, side by side
matrix.lede: One representative product per category. Presence of a capability, as of mid-2026, from public vendor documentation.
matrix.legend: ✓ ships this capability · ~ partial, or leaders-only · ✗ not shipped
matrix.note: Capability presence as of mid-2026, compiled from public vendor documentation; products are representative of their category, not exhaustive. Cells reflect a shipped capability, not an endorsement or a quality score. OpenWOP's real-time multiplayer builder is available behind an operator toggle, so it is marked partial. Corrections welcome — this is a living comparison, not a benchmark.

outro.heading: Runs you can trust, on data you can see
outro.body: Every OpenWOP workflow — whether a chain of nodes or a stack of todos — runs on one executor whose runs pin their version, replay deterministically, and fork from any step. That is what lets AI authoring, cost budgets, and a human-in-the-loop ladder ride on top without a determinism tax. The comparison above is a snapshot; the moat is the substrate underneath it.
